original_question: Classify all self-inverting polynomials and formal power series whose inversion pair equals the series itself, and in particular classify all such examples that are Hessian nilpotent.
target_in_paper: Section 4, Open Problem 4.8(a)-(b): (a) decide whether all self-inverting polynomials or formal power series are Hessian nilpotent; (b) classify all (HN) self-inverting polynomials and formal power series.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the Section 4 theme of self-inverting objects, uses the right basic meaning of self-inverting as having inversion pair equal to the original series, and notices that the paper singles out the Hessian nilpotent subclass as the main classification target.
missing_details: The paper works over the complex numbers: polynomials in C[z] and formal power series in C[[z]].
The variables are multivariate, z=(z_1,...,z_n), with n arbitrary but finite.
In Section 4, 'self-inverting' is not a bare condition Q=P for an arbitrary series; Definition 4.1 includes the hypotheses o(P) >= 2 and (Hes P)(0) nilpotent.
The paper's exact target is not only classification of HN self-inverting examples; Open Problem 4.8 also asks first whether every self-inverting polynomial or formal power series is automatically HN.
You should define the inversion pair Q(z): it is the series for which the symmetric formal map F(z)=z-∇P(z) has formal inverse G(z)=z+∇Q(z).
The nearby context in Section 4 gives an equivalent criterion: under o(P) >= 2 and (Hes P)(0) nilpotent, P is self-inverting iff <∇P,∇P>=0.
The paper also gives an equivalent reformulation via the deformed inversion pair Q_t(z): self-inverting iff Q_t(z)=P(z).
The draft does not distinguish clearly between 'all self-inverting' and '(HN) self-inverting'; in the paper this distinction is exactly the content of Open Problem 4.8(a) versus 4.8(b).
The question should state explicitly that HN means the Hessian matrix Hes P(z) is nilpotent.
The phrase 'whose inversion pair equals the series itself' is redundant once 'self-inverting' has been defined.
refined_question: Let z=(z_1,\dots,z_n), and let P(z) be either a polynomial in C[z] or a formal power series in C[[z]] with o(P)\ge 2 and (Hes\,P)(0) nilpotent. Let Q(z) denote the inversion pair of P, defined by requiring that the symmetric formal map F(z)=z-\nabla P(z) have formal inverse G(z)=z+\nabla Q(z). If P is self-inverting, i.e. Q(z)=P(z), is P necessarily Hessian nilpotent? More generally, classify all self-inverting polynomials and formal power series, and in particular classify all Hessian nilpotent self-inverting polynomials and formal power series.
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, under the same hypotheses o(P)\ge 2 and (Hes\,P)(0) nilpotent, classify those P for which the deformed inversion pair Q_t(z) satisfies Q_t(z)=P(z).
justification: Section 1.2 explicitly says that one purpose of Section 4 is to draw attention to an open classification problem for HN self-inverting polynomials or formal power series. In Section 4, Definition 4.1 fixes the hidden hypotheses under which 'self-inverting' is used. Proposition 4.3 then gives the paper's main local characterization of self-inverting series in this setup, namely self-inverting iff <∇P,∇P>=0. After presenting a known family of HN self-inverting examples in Example 4.7, the paper states Open Problem 4.8, whose official formulation has exactly the two parts reflected above: first the HN-versus-self-inverting question, and then the classification of (HN) self-inverting polynomials and formal power series. Proposition 4.9 explicitly proves the equivalent formulation using the deformed inversion pair Q_t(z).
